prompt: Estimate how long customers stay subscribed, when most current customers haven't cancelled yet.
why: Still-active customers are censored; Kaplan–Meier or Cox models handle them correctly.
trap: Dropping active customers, or treating them as churned, biases the estimate.

prompt: Estimate when pumps are likely to fail. Most pumps in the field are still running.
tells: when pumps are likely to fail
why: Time-to-event with censoring: model the hazard of failure over time.
trap: Anomaly detection spots odd behavior now; this predicts when failure comes.

prompt: Does being on the annual plan change how quickly customers cancel, accounting for those still subscribed?
why: A Cox proportional hazards model gives a hazard ratio for the plan type.
trap: Logistic regression on "cancelled yes/no" ignores when it happened.

prompt: Recruiting wants the median time to fill a role, but a third of open roles are still unfilled.
tells: median time to fill a role
why: Kaplan–Meier estimates the median while respecting the unfilled (censored) roles.
trap: Averaging only filled roles makes it look faster than it is.

prompt: Estimate how long new hires typically stay, when most people hired in the last two years still work here.
tells: how long new hires typically stay
why: Current employees are censored observations; Kaplan–Meier handles them.
trap: Averaging only people who left makes tenure look short.

prompt: Compare time to relapse between two treatment groups in a trial where many patients hadn't relapsed when the study ended.
tells: hadn't relapsed when the study ended
why: Kaplan–Meier curves per group compared with a log-rank test.
trap: It's a randomized comparison, but the outcome is time-to-event with censoring.

prompt: For each active subscriber, estimate the risk of cancelling in the next 30 days given their tenure and usage so far.
tells: risk of cancelling in the next 30 days
why: A hazard model conditions on having survived so far, which suits tenure-dependent risk.
trap: A plain classifier can work, but it ignores how risk changes with tenure.

prompt: Estimate how many laptops will need a repair within 3 years, from units sold over the past 18 months.
why: Most units haven't been owned 3 years yet; model time-to-failure with censoring and extrapolate.
trap: Forecasting sales isn't the question; failure timing is.
